query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Directional solidification with a tailored cooling rate followed by subcritical annealing will refine the eutectic lamellar microstructure in high-entropy alloys, thereby simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility relative to the as‐cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy) with a fine lamellar microstructure of alternating soft FCC and hard B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Apply directional solidification with controlled cooling rates to achieve aligned, refined lamellae followed by a subcritical annealing step to relieve residual stresses and improve interphase interface coherence.
generation.conditions: Under ambient (room temperature) mechanical loading conditions typical of structural applications, with processing parameters optimized to avoid coarsening or embrittlement.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced interlamellar spacing and enhanced interphase bonding (improved coherence at FCC/B2 interfaces) that reduce stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: Directional solidification provides a more uniformly aligned and refined eutectic structure, while subcritical annealing relieves residual stresses and promotes slight recovery at the interfaces. Together, these changes lower the propensity for crack initiation and propagation, thereby boosting both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventionally cast alloys, samples processed with this intervention are expected to exhibit a measurable increase in yield (or fracture) strength and a higher fracture strain (ductility) without the typical trade-off encountered in strength-ductility optimization.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy featuring the conventional fine lamellar microstructure achieved by standard casting methods.
generation.boundary: This approach is effective only when processing parameters (cooling rate and annealing temperature/time) are carefully optimized to maintain the delicate balance of phase fractions without causing coarsening, grain growth, or undesired phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the mechanical improvements is uncertain as it depends on precise process parameter tuning and alloy-specific behavior. Additional work is required to define the optimal processing window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with the same composition: one set using conventional as-cast processing and the other using the proposed directional solidification with tailored cooling followed by subcritical annealing. Utilize scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to characterize the microstructure (paying attention to the interlamellar spacing and phase interface coherence). Conduct tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture strain under identical conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to measure lamellar spacing and interface quality.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess residual stress relief and phase retention.
Tensile testing to record yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture strain.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directional solidification plus subcritical annealing samples do not exhibit statistically significant simultaneous increases in both strength and ductility as compared with the conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] . HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in th

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. chosen.technique: directional solidification with controlled cooling followed by standardized annealing (e.g., annealing at 900°C for 1h)

chosen.why: This intervention directly fills the open question by modifying phase architecture through established thermal treatments. It leverages standard techniques in thermal/thermomechanical treatment to achieve simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility by refining the microstructural features of eutectic high-entropy alloys, with clear process parameters and reproducible conditions.

frame.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (HEAs) developed for structural applications, typically comprising alternating soft and hard phases with a fine eutectic microstructure as the starting state.
frame.goal: Simultaneously increase both strength and ductility relative to a baseline alloy (where modifications lead to trade‐offs, e.g., strengthening that typically sacrifices ductility).
frame.limitation: The inherent trade-off in eutectic HEAs between strength and ductility due to microstructural constraints, where conventional interventions often improve one property at the expense of the other.
constraints: The intervention must be applicable to the existing eutectic microstructure and alloy chemistry
It must yield measurable improvement relative to an established baseline
frame.regime: Tests conducted under structural loading conditions, typically at room temperature with strain rates that simulate real-world mechanical applications.
prior_attempts: Optimization of alloy composition through additional elements to enhance strength often led to embrittlement or reduced ductility
Thermo-mechanical treatments and precipitation strengthening processes have been used, yet they tend to favor one property over the other
Microstructural refinement via processing routes has improved one aspect (e.g., strength) but at the expense of the toughness or ductility

decision.trend: The early work on eutectic HEAs, exemplified by the 2014 AlCoCrFeNi study (PMC4145285), revealed that the as‐cast fine lamellar microstructure can provide a decent balance of strength and ductility; however, interventions such as cold rolling improved strength at the cost of ductility. In parallel, work on other HEA systems—often via composition adjustments or precipitation strengthening—has generally enhanced one property while compromising the other. The trend shows that while thermomechanical tuning and processing modifications have been attempted, controlling the interlamellar spacing and interface coherence in eutectic systems without sacrificing ductility remains a challenge.
decision.unsolved: How to implement a single processing intervention that optimally refines the eutectic structure to simultaneously boost strength and ductility without triggering the usual trade-off remains unresolved.
decision.lever: directional solidification with tailored cooling rates combined with post-solidification subcritical annealing
decision.why: This lever directly builds on the effective use of thermomechanical processing while targeting the key microstructural parameters—eutectic spacing and interphase interface quality—that govern both strength and ductility. The proposed directional solidification approach would allow for controlled phase spacing and alignment in the eutectic microstructure, while the subcritical annealing step helps in relieving residual stresses and fine-tuning the phase connectivity. This integration, inspired by prior successes of processing modifications yet acknowledging their limitations, offers a promising, testable pathway that occupies the experimental niche addressing the open question.
